CHAPTER 1
INTRODUCTION
1.1 Project Context

Effective inventory management remains one of the most significant challenges in retail businesses, particularly in stores that experience high daily transaction volumes and frequent inventory movement. Shalom Store in Tangub City processes an average of 400 customer  transactions per day, manages approximately 1,200 active products, and replenishes its inventory twice a week to meet customer demand. In addition, the store offers a wide variety of merchandise across multiple product categories, including groceries, beverages, canned goods, snacks, personal care products, school and office supplies, and other consumer goods. The broad assortment of products, combined with frequent customer transactions and regular inventory replenishment, increases the complexity of monitoring inventory levels, identifying fast-moving products, and maintaining sufficient stock availability.

For the purposes of this study, a high-volume department store is operationally defined as a retail establishment that experiences a high frequency of daily customer transactions, manages a large number of active products, offers merchandise across multiple product categories, and requires frequent inventory replenishment due to continuous product movement. Based on this operational definition, Shalom Store was selected as the study site because it processes approximately 400 customer transactions daily, maintains around 1,200 active products, carries a diverse range of merchandise, and restocks its inventory twice a week. Although the store operates on a smaller scale than large national retail chains, its operational characteristics and inventory management requirements are comparable to those of a high-volume department store, making it an appropriate environment for implementing and evaluating the proposed AI-driven inventory management and demand forecasting system.

Like many retail businesses, the store faces challenges such as stock-outs, overstocking, delayed inventory updates, and difficulty predicting future product demand. These issues may result in lost sales opportunities, increased inventory holding costs, inefficient replenishment decisions, and reduced customer satisfaction. According to Blair (2023), inventory distortion caused by stock-outs, overstocking, and inventory shrinkage was projected to cost retailers approximately $1.77 trillion globally in 2023, emphasizing the importance of adopting more effective inventory management strategies.

If these inventory management problems remain unresolved, retailers may continue to experience lost sales opportunities, unnecessary inventory holding costs, inefficient stock replenishment, and poor customer service. Managers often struggle to make timely inventory decisions because they rely on outdated or incomplete inventory information, particularly during periods of fluctuating customer demand. These challenges become even more critical in high-volume department stores where frequent inventory transactions and continuous stock movement make manual monitoring increasingly difficult and prone to human error.

Recent studies suggest that Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning have become effective technologies for improving inventory management. According to Sekhar (2024), AI significantly enhances demand forecasting, stock optimization, and automated replenishment by analyzing historical sales records, seasonal demand, market trends, and customer purchasing behavior. Similarly, machine learning techniques enable forecasting models to learn from historical sales data and continuously improve prediction accuracy, allowing retailers to anticipate future demand more effectively and make data-driven inventory decisions.

Despite the availability of computerized inventory systems, many existing solutions primarily focus on inventory recording, stock monitoring, and report generation while providing limited predictive capabilities for future demand. This study aims to develop RetailMind: An AI-Driven Inventory Management and Demand Forecasting System for High-Volume Department Stores for Shalom Store in Tangub City. Specifically, the system seeks to analyze historical sales data, generate demand forecasts, provide low-stock notifications, and assist store personnel in making timely, data-driven inventory decisions that reduce stock-outs and overstocking while improving operational efficiency.

The proposed web-based system integrates a Random Forest Regressor  as its demand forecasting model. RFR is a supervised ensemble machine-learning algorithm that builds multiple decision trees using samples of the available data and combines their predictions to produce a final demand estimate. This approach enables the model to identify complex and nonlinear relationships among historical sales , sales trends, days of the week, months, and relevant calendar-based events. By combining the predictions of multiple trees, the model can provide stable forecasts while reducing the possibility that individual data patterns will excessively influence the results.

The Random Forest Regressor was selected because retail demand can be affected by interacting factors and may vary across products, categories, dates, and seasonal periods. Its ability to process several predictor variables and identify complex sales patterns makes it suitable for Shalom Store’s diverse inventory and transaction data. The forecasting model may be periodically retrained using newly accumulated sales records so that its predictions remain responsive to changing demand patterns. Its generated forecasts and replenishment recommendations will function as decision-support information, while final restocking decisions will remain under the control of authorized Inventory Managers.

The proposed system also contributes to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals by supporting Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure under SDG 9 through the application of artificial intelligence and digital technologies to modernize retail inventory operations. It advances Responsible Consumption and Production under SDG 12 by providing demand forecasts and replenishment recommendations that can help reduce unnecessary overstocking, stock shortages, and potential product waste. Furthermore, RetailMind supports Decent Work and Economic Growth under SDG 8 by improving operational efficiency and assisting store personnel in making timely, informed, and data-driven inventory decisions.

Through real-time inventory monitoring, Random Forest-based demand forecasting, low-stock notifications, inventory analytics, and replenishment recommendations, RetailMind aims to reduce stock-outs and overstocking, improve inventory accuracy, and support timely inventory planning. The proposed system is expected to provide Shalom Store with a more organized, data-driven, and efficient approach to managing its inventory operations.
1.2 Purpose and Description

This project aims to develop a web-based AI-driven inventory management and demand forecasting system designed specifically for Shalom Store, a high-volume department store in Tangub City. The proposed system seeks to address the challenges associated with manual inventory monitoring and optimize inventory operations by providing a centralized platform for managing inventory records, monitoring stock movements, and forecasting future product demand using artificial intelligence.

RetailMind: An AI-Driven Inventory Management and Demand Forecasting System for High-Volume Department Store is intended to improve inventory management by enabling store personnel to monitor stock levels in real time, analyze historical sales data, and receive demand forecasting insights that support timely inventory replenishment decisions. The system functions as a decision support system by providing Inventory Managers with data-driven forecasts and replenishment recommendations while leaving the final inventory decisions to authorized personnel. The forecasting model will initially start collecting store sales data for a period of time due for the reason that there is no available store historical sale data for the initial set up and are designed to be periodically updated as new transaction data become available, allowing the system to improve its demand forecasting capability over time. Through this predictive capability, RetailMind aims to reduce stock-outs, minimize overstocking, improve inventory accuracy, and support informed decision-making. The generated forecasts serve as recommendations rather than automatic decisions, assisting Inventory Managers in evaluating replenishment needs, maintaining appropriate stock levels, and improving overall operational efficiency

This system will serve as a web-based information system that centralizes inventory-related activities and provides authorized users with convenient access to inventory information. By integrating inventory management with AI-based demand forecasting, the proposed system aims to provide Shalom Store with a more efficient, accurate, and intelligent approach to managing inventory while supporting better operational planning, inventory control, and customer service.

1.4 Scope and Limitations of the Project

Shalom Store is a high-volume retail establishment located in Tangub City that processes approximately 400 customer transactions daily, manages around 1,200 active products across multiple categories, and replenishes its inventory twice a week. RetailMind: An AI-Driven Inventory Management and Demand Forecasting System for High-Volume Department Store is a web-based system designed specifically for the store’s inventory operations and is accessible through desktop and mobile web browsers.

The system supports supports four role workspaces for platform governance, Store administration, inventory management and cashier operations. Its scope covers product and batch inventory, direct stock receiving, physical counts, Stock Issue review, cashier shifts, sales, Receipt History, authorized refunds and corrections, manual GCash services, reports, notifications and audit records. Manual GCash services record reference numbers, fees and internal cash and wallet reconciliation. Staff perform the external GCash transfer separately. Cost-based profit reporting depends on recorded purchase costs.

The Random Forest pipeline estimates recorded sales through a 28-day horizon, with evaluation summaries for 7, 14 and 28-day totals. The current feature set excludes category attributes, prices, promotions and local-event indicators. Forecasts and stock-rule suggestions remain advisory and are labeled by their basis. Training, quality checks, technical and operational review and completed observation evidence are separate from history-readiness labels.

The project is limited to the inventory management and demand forecasting operations of Shalom Store. Forecast accuracy depends on the availability, consistency, completeness, and representativeness of the historical sales data. Sudden changes in customer behavior, natural disasters, market disruptions, supplier shortages, theft, or damaged inventory may reduce forecasting accuracy. The local installation depends on the Store PC, server, database and configured network. Internet access is required for external services such as email and externally hosted assets. Finalized sales remain historical records, while authorized refunds and corrections use linked records rather than silently replacing the original transaction.

1.6 Definition of Terms
The following terms are defined conceptually and operationally as they are used within the context of this study:

Artificial Intelligence (AI). It refers to computer technology that performs tasks requiring intelligent decision-making. This refers to RetailMind's capability to analyze historical sales data and generate demand forecasts using a Random Forest Regressor.

Barcode Scanner. It refers to an electronic device used to read barcode labels for product identification. This refers to the device used in RetailMind to record stock-in, stock-out, and sales transactions accurately.

Demand Forecasting. It refers to the process of estimating future customer demand using historical data. In this implementation, demand forecasting estimates expected recorded product sales for replenishment planning; it does not directly measure all customer demand lost during shortages.

Inventory Management. It refers to the process of monitoring and controlling product inventory. This refers to RetailMind's functions for tracking stock levels, recording inventory movements, and managing inventory records.

Machine Learning (ML). It refers to a field of artificial intelligence that enables systems to learn from historical data. This refers to the technology used by RetailMind to identify sales patterns and generate demand forecasts.
Overstock. It refers to a condition in which inventory exceeds customer demand. This refers to products identified by RetailMind as having stock levels higher than forecasted demand.

Random Forest Regressor (RFR). It refers to a supervised ensemble machine-learning algorithm that combines predictions from multiple decision trees to estimate a continuous numerical value. In RetailMind, the Random Forest Regressor uses product identity, forecast step, sales lags, rolling sales statistics and target-date indicators to estimate recorded sales in Base Units.

Replenishment. It refers to the process of restoring inventory to the required stock level. This refers to RetailMind's recommendations for restocking products based on forecasted demand and current inventory levels.

RetailMind. It refers to an AI-driven inventory management and demand forecasting system. This refers to the proposed web-based system that monitors inventory, records stock transactions, and forecasts product demand for Shalom Store.

Stock-out. It refers to a condition in which a product is unavailable due to insufficient inventory. This refers to RetailMind's detection of low or zero stock levels and generation of low-stock alerts.

Comparative evaluations of retail demand forecasting models further justify the use of ensemble tree-based algorithms over traditional linear and standalone statistical models. In the M5 Forecasting accuracy benchmark analyzed by Makridakis et al. (2022), machine learning methods that combine lagged sales series, rolling statistical aggregates, and calendar variables consistently outperformed traditional univariate time-series approaches across multi-item retail datasets. Unlike Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), which assumes a strictly linear relationship between predictors and target demand, or Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), which requires training and tuning a separate parameter set for every individual product, a global Random Forest Regressor (RFR) learns cross-product demand behaviors simultaneously within a single unified model.

Similarly, empirical retail forecasting studies by Googerdchi and Jafari (2025) and Zavaleta-Zarate et al. (2026) highlight that the Random Forest Regressor mitigates overfitting in noisy daily retail transactions through bootstrap aggregating (bagging). Because daily retail logs frequently exhibit zero-sale days interspersed with sudden multi-unit purchases, single decision trees and linear models are highly sensitive to transaction variance. By constructing an ensemble of decorrelated decision trees and averaging their predictions across multi-day horizons (such as 14-day and 28-day replenishment windows), RFR smooths out daily transaction noise and provides stable demand estimates suitable for physical store restocking.

The reviewed inventory management systems demonstrate that modern inventory solutions have significantly improved inventory control through features such as real-time stock monitoring, inventory tracking, automated stock replenishment, inventory reporting, and demand planning. 3.1.1 Research Design

The development of the proposed system follows the Agile Scrum software development methodology, which supports an iterative and collaborative approach to system development. Through incremental development cycles, this methodology allows the proponents to continuously refine the system based on stakeholder feedback and changing requirements. It also helps ensure that the proposed system remains aligned with the operational needs of Shalom Store while maintaining flexibility throughout the development process.

Agile Software Development Model

The development process begins with Requirements Gathering, during which interviews, observations, and consultations are conducted to identify the client’s inventory management practices, operational challenges, and system requirements. This is followed by the Design and Development phases, in which the system architecture, database, user interface, and web application are designed and implemented using PHP, HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and MySQL.

During development, a Python-based Random Forest Regressor (RFR), implemented using the Scikit-learn library, is integrated into the system. The model analyzes historical sales data using 14 engineered predictor variables—including product and horizon identifiers, autoregressive sales lags, rolling demand statistics, and calendar indicators—to generate 7-, 14-, and 28-day demand forecasts that support inventory replenishment planning.

After development, the system undergoes Testing, Deployment, and Review to ensure that its functions operate according to the specified requirements. Functional testing, integration testing, forecast accuracy testing, and User Acceptance Testing (UAT) are conducted to evaluate the system’s reliability, usability, integration, and forecasting performance.

Following deployment, RetailMind is continuously refined through stakeholder feedback, software enhancements, and development iterations. The Random Forest Regressor may also be periodically retrained using newly recorded sales data to keep its forecasts responsive to changing demand patterns and ensure that the system continues to support the operational requirements of Shalom Store.

Instead, inventory records are manually maintained in a physical logbook by the inventory manager. To determine current stock levels, the inventory manager conducts periodic physical stock counts and manually compares the remaining inventory with the entries recorded in the logbook.

Based on these manually maintained records, the inventory manager determines when products require replenishment. Reordering decisions rely heavily on personal experience, observed remaining stock during physical inspections, and historical sales records. Due to the absence of real-time monitoring, automated inventory updates, and demand forecasting capabilities, low-stock situations are often identified only when inventory levels are already critically low. As a result, the existing manual process is time-consuming, prone to human error, and may lead to stock-outs, overstocking, inaccurate inventory records, and delays in inventory-related decision-making.

text: 3.2.2 Functional Requirements

The proposed RetailMind shall provide four workspaces for the Super Administrator, Administrator, Inventory Manager and Cashier. The application shall authenticate users and enforce the permissions of the active workspace. The Super Administrator shall manage technical platform settings and maintenance. The Store Administrator shall oversee delegated staff accounts, fiscal periods, operational reviews and eligible model approval.

The system shall provide a role-based dashboard that displays relevant information, including inventory summaries, low-stock notifications, recent transactions, sales trends, and demand forecasting results. Inventory Managers shall be able to add, update, archive, search, filter, and organize products and product categories. The system shall monitor inventory levels in real time and identify products as available, low-stock, or out-of-stock based on their recorded quantities and predefined minimum stock levels.

The Inventory Manager shall maintain product and stock records, record direct receiving, review physical counts and Stock Issues, and consult buying guidance. The Cashier shall record sales through an authorized shift, access permitted receipts, submit Stock Issues and record authorized manual GCash services. Finalized sales shall be preserved in Receipt History. Authorized refunds and corrections shall be recorded as linked transactions.

The forecasting pipeline shall use a Random Forest Regressor to estimate recorded sales within a 28-day horizon. The workspace shall display 7-, 14- and 28-day totals where eligible forecast output exists. Stock-rule suggestions shall be identified separately. Buying guidance shall remain advisory, and goods received shall be recorded through Direct Stock Receiving.

The forecasting module shall be developed using Python and the Scikit-learn library and integrated with the PHP-based web application. The Random Forest Regressor shall be trained using historical sales records and periodically retrained using newly recorded sales data. The generated forecasts shall be stored in the system and displayed through the dashboard and demand forecasting reports.

Based on forecasted demand, current inventory quantities, and predefined stock thresholds, the system shall provide replenishment recommendations to assist Inventory Managers in making timely restocking decisions. These recommendations shall function only as decision-support information, and final replenishment decisions shall remain under the authority of the Inventory Manager. The system shall also support CSV file imports for the efficient processing and updating of multiple product records.

RetailMind shall generate printable and exportable reports, including inventory summaries, stock movement reports, sales reports, low-stock reports, overstock reports, and demand forecasting reports. The system shall maintain an audit trail of user activities, including login sessions, inventory modifications, sales transactions, forecasting activities, and account management actions, for monitoring, accountability, and security purposes.

The System Administrator shall be able to manage fiscal periods by opening and closing inventory tracking cycles. Closed fiscal periods shall become read-only to preserve the integrity of historical records. The system shall also automatically send email notifications to Inventory Managers regarding low-stock products and significant changes in forecasted demand.
3.2.3 Non-Functional Requirements

RetailMind shall provide a user-friendly, secure, and responsive web-based environment for inventory management and demand forecasting. The interface shall enable users with minimal technical knowledge to perform authorized tasks using desktop and mobile web browsers. User and business information shall be protected through secure authentication, encrypted passwords, session management, and role-based access control. Relevant user activities shall also be recorded in an audit log for accountability and security monitoring.

RetailMind protects account credentials through password hashing and enforces authenticated sessions and role-based access controls. Desktop and mobile browsers access the application through the Store server.

The forecasting component shall generate product-demand predictions using a trained Random Forest Regressor and selected historical, product-related, and calendar-based predictor variables. Forecasting performance shall be evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), where lower values indicate better forecasting accuracy. Generated forecasts and replenishment recommendations shall function only as decision-support information and shall not automatically perform inventory transactions.

RetailMind supports encrypted Database Backup packages and local restoration. An authorized Administrator or Super Administrator confirms replacement with their current login password. The restoration workflow checks the package and destination, handles account conflicts, creates a destination safety copy and pauses Store writes. The Store is reopened after verification and explicit confirmation. It shall be accessible to authorized users through an internet connection whenever the application server is available. The system shall accommodate increasing numbers of users, products, inventory transactions, and historical sales records without significantly affecting normal performance. A modular architecture shall support maintenance, software updates, bug fixes, security improvements, future enhancements, and periodic retraining of the Random Forest Regressor. Database backups and recovery procedures shall also be maintained to reduce the risk of permanent data loss and support the system’s long-term reliability.

text: 3.4 Development and Testing
3.4.1 Development

The proponents adopted the Agile Scrum development methodology to develop RetailMind, a web-based inventory management and demand forecasting system designed for Shalom Store. Agile Scrum enabled iterative development, continuous stakeholder feedback, and incremental improvements throughout the project lifecycle, ensuring that the system remained aligned with the operational requirements of the client.

The development process began with requirements gathering through interviews and observations of Shalom Store's existing inventory management practices. This phase identified challenges related to inventory monitoring, sales recording, stock replenishment, and demand forecasting. Based on the gathered requirements, the proponents designed the system architecture, database schema, user interface, and process flow. The web application was developed using PHP, HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Bootstrap, and MySQL, while the demand forecasting component was implemented using Python and the Scikit-learn library. The forecasting module utilizes a Random Forest Regressor (RFR) model that analyzes historical sales data using 14 engineered predictor features (product_id, horizon_day, lag_1, lag_7, lag_14, lag_28, rolling_mean_7, rolling_std_7, rolling_mean_28, rolling_std_28, day_of_week, day_of_month, month, and is_weekend) across 7-, 14-, and 28-day horizons. During model training, these predictor variables are automatically extracted from historical sales records, product information, and calendar data stored in the database, eliminating the need for additional manual data entry.

The developed system consists of several integrated modules, including user management, inventory management, barcode-supported product registration, sales transaction recording, inventory transactions, demand forecasting, inventory reporting, audit logging, notification services, and replenishment recommendation generation. As new sales transactions are recorded, they are stored in the database and become part of the historical sales dataset used for periodic retraining of the Random Forest model, allowing the forecasting module to improve its predictions as more sales data become available. Each completed module underwent continuous testing and refinement to verify functionality, usability, system integration, and forecasting performance. Feedback gathered during each Agile sprint was incorporated into subsequent iterations to ensure that the final system satisfied the project's functional and non-functional requirements before deployment.
3.4.2 Machine Learning Training Pipeline

To validate the predictive capability of the Random Forest Regressor (RFR) before live store activation, the proponents implemented a reproducible training and evaluation pipeline in Google Colab using Python, pandas (v2.2.3), numpy, pyarrow, and scikit-learn. Because Shalom Store previously relied on manual physical logbooks without digitized item-level daily sales histories, pre-deployment model benchmarking was conducted using a pinned subset of the public M5 retail dataset (50 products from the CA_1 FOODS retail store category across 730 training days from March 1, 2014 to February 28, 2016), while enforcing a strict integration boundary so that public benchmark data remain completely isolated from Shalom Store's production database.

The model is trained on two years of historical daily sales (730 days), the subsequent two 28-day chronological blocks are used solely as validation folds to calibrate the sale-day classification threshold (set at 0.5), and the final held-out 28-day window serves as the unseen Testing Set. 3.4.2 Testing
3.4.2.1 Alpha Testing

To ensure the quality, reliability, and functionality of RetailMind, the proponents conducted both Alpha Testing and Beta Testing. Alpha Testing was performed internally to verify that all modules function correctly before release. Beta Testing was then conducted with the intended users of the system to evaluate its usability, functionality, reliability, and overall performance under actual operating conditions.
3.4.2.2 Forecast Accuracy Testing

The demand forecasting module underwent Forecast Accuracy Testing in Google Colab to evaluate the predictive performance of the Random Forest Regressor (RFR) against the Seasonal Naive baseline before operational deployment. Model performance across 7-day, 14-day, and 28-day horizons was evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Weighted Absolute Percentage Error (WAPE), and Any-Sale-Day Classification F1-Score. Furthermore, to ensure safe operational deployment at Shalom Store, the system enforces strict Data Readiness bands based on accumulated local store history: below 56 days (Insufficient), 56–179 days (Low), 180–364 days (Medium), and 365+ days (High, subject to chronological validation pass).

text: 4.3.2.1 Forecast Accuracy Testing Results (Google Colab Training & Validation)

Prior to activating live store forecasts, the proponents executed the demand forecasting experiment in Google Colab (m5_sales_experiment.py) using 50 retail products over a two-year training window (March 1, 2014 to February 28, 2016, totaling 730 days) and evaluated the trained Random Forest Regressor (RFR) on the final unseen 28-day test window (Fold 3). The model was trained using the 14 engineered predictor variables (product_id, horizon_day, lag_1, lag_7, lag_14, lag_28, rolling_mean_7, rolling_std_7, rolling_mean_28, rolling_std_28, day_of_week, day_of_month, month, and is_weekend) and compared directly against the Seasonal Naive baseline (predicting the previous week's sales). Table 12 presents the comparative forecast accuracy results across the 7-day, 14-day, and 28-day test horizons.
Table 12
Comparative Forecast Accuracy Results: Random Forest Regressor vs. Seasonal Naive Baseline (50 Products, Fold 3 Test Split)

Note: MAE and RMSE measure per-product horizon unit totals across the 50 evaluated products, not single-day errors. WAPE represents the aggregate absolute error as a percentage of total actual units sold (lower values indicate higher forecasting accuracy).
As shown in Table 12, the forecasting evaluation reveals an important operational insight across replenishment horizons:

The public M5 holdout provides benchmark evidence for the selected products. Seasonal Naive recorded lower error at 7 days, while Random Forest recorded lower error at 14 and 28 days. At 28 days, reported WAPE was 29.63% for Random Forest and 36.53% for Seasonal Naive. Aggregate results can mask weak forecasts for individual products. Any-sale-day classification measures the identification of sale days, and a missed sale day does not establish that a stock-out occurred.

RetailMind classifies Store history by usable days: Insufficient below 56, Low from 56 to 179, Medium from 180 to 364 and High at 365 or more. Closures, stock-outs and missing evidence are handled separately. Candidate qualification uses chronological evaluation against the baseline and configured quality gates. Prospective observation and local Administrator approval are separate requirements.
Table 13
Any-Sale-Day Classification Performance on Held-Out Test Set (Threshold = 0.5)

As presented in Table 13, the Random Forest model achieved the highest F1-Score (0.7525) and a 93.14% recall on active sale days, recording only 56 False Negatives compared to 272 False Negatives under the Seasonal Naive baseline. In a retail inventory context, minimizing False Negatives is critical because a False Negative represents an unpredicted sale day that can directly trigger a shelf stock-out.
Per-Product Error Analysis, Model Limitations, and Integration Safeguards

While the Random Forest Regressor outperformed the baseline across the aggregate 50-product portfolio on the 14-day and 28-day horizons (improving 28-day absolute error over the baseline for 28 out of 50 products), per-product diagnostic inspection revealed that RFR did not beat the simple baseline for 22 out of 50 products. This finding justifies two critical architectural safeguards built directly into the RetailMind web application:

1. Forecast Exceptions Queue & WAPE Alert Threshold (35%): Because aggregate metrics can mask weak predictions on individual erratic items, RetailMind includes a dedicated Forecast Exceptions module. Any product whose validation WAPE exceeds the 35% threshold or fails to beat the 7-day baseline is automatically flagged in the exception queue for manual review by the Inventory Manager.

2. Operational Data Readiness & Stock-Out Blind-Spot Mitigation: Pure historical sales records cannot distinguish between zero customer demand and zero shelf inventory (stock-outs). Unlike public benchmark datasets that lack physical stock-out logs, RetailMind's MySQL database natively records real-time inventory balances, stock issue reports, Cost/Sales prices, promotions, and Store Calendar closures. In production at Shalom Store, the public M5 demonstration data remain strictly isolated; local model activation requires accumulating sufficient store transaction history across the system's Data Readiness bands (<56 days: Insufficient; 56–179 days: Low; 180–364 days: Medium; 365+ days: High) and passing chronological validation before assisting the Inventory Manager with replenishment decisions.
Chapter V
SUMMARY, CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATION
5.1 SUMMARY

RetailMind integrates inventory, receiving, checkout and forecasting workflows for Shalom Store. Four workspaces separate platform governance, Store administration, inventory management and cashier operations. The system maintains traceable stock movements, saved receipts, linked refunds and operational records. Buying guidance combines eligible forecast output or stock rules with recorded inventory information to support decisions by authorized personnel.

The public M5 benchmark showed that Random Forest produced lower error than Seasonal Naive at the reported 14- and 28-day horizons, while Seasonal Naive performed better at 7 days. Isolated tests demonstrated the operation of the forecasting pipeline. The reported evidence for installed unattended operation and predictive usefulness on genuine Store outcomes was still incomplete.
5.2 CONCLUSION
Based on the development, pre-deployment model validation, and operational testing of RetailMind for Shalom Store in Tangub City, the proponents formulated the following conclusions:

Transitioning Shalom Store from manual physical logbooks to a centralized, role-based web application across four workspaces (Super Administrator, Administrator, Inventory Manager, and Cashier) streamlines barcode-assisted POS checkout, real-time stock monitoring, direct stock receiving, physical inventory counts, and manual GCash transaction logging.

Pre-deployment benchmarking of the 14-feature Random Forest Regressor (RFR) pipeline in Google Colab using a 50-product subset of the M5 retail dataset across 730 training days demonstrated that while the Seasonal Naive baseline yielded lower error on noisy 7-day horizons (37.88% vs. 43.00% WAPE), the Random Forest Regressor outperformed the baseline on 14-day (32.44% vs. 37.71% WAPE) and 28-day (29.63% vs. 36.53% WAPE) replenishment horizons, while achieving a 93.14% recall (0.7525 F1-Score) in active sale-day classification.

Integrating architectural safeguards—specifically the Forecast Data Readiness bands (<56 days: Insufficient up to 365+ days: High), the 35% WAPE Forecast Exceptions queue, and Stock-Rule Replenishment Suggestions—ensures that Shalom Store receives reliable inventory buying guidance during the initial cold-start data collection phase without contaminating live store records with external benchmark data.
5.3 RECOMMENDATION
Based on the findings and limitations of the study, the following recommendations are proposed:

Continuous POS Data Accumulation for Local Model Activation: Shalom Store personnel should consistently record all daily checkout transactions, stock receiving entries, and physical counts in RetailMind so products can progress past the 56-day Data Readiness threshold and activate live 14-day and 28-day Random Forest demand forecasts.

Focus on 14-Day and 28-Day Replenishment Horizons: Store management should utilize the 14-day and 28-day forecast summaries alongside Stock-Rule Suggestions for bi-weekly and monthly purchasing decisions, while using the Forecast Exceptions module to manually review erratic items exceeding the 35% WAPE threshold.

Future Feature Expansion: Future researchers and developers may expand the 14-feature forecasting pipeline by incorporating recorded product category attributes, unit price changes, active store promotions, and local Tangub City calendar events once sufficient multi-year store transaction history has been accumulated.
